gloss_distractors: the members of a trade union
senses.definition: The most senior people in an organisation, as described by people who work under them.
senses.caution: It is informal and shows you are not one of them. In formal writing say the executive committee, and do not use it when talking to senior people directly.
senses.example: The brass are in the building on Thursday, so keep the demo to ten minutes and skip the architecture slide.

cues.text: You are warning your team in a channel that the most senior leaders in the firm will be sitting in on Thursday's review, and you want the informal collective for them.
Over coffee a peer asks who actually killed the project, and the answer is the most senior people in the firm, whom neither of you has ever met. You want the informal phrase for them.
A friend complains that the decision to close her branch came from people at head office who have never once visited it.
Your uncle is telling army stories about the officers who came round for inspection, and you want the wry phrase for them.

distractors: A committee formed to review one decision and then dissolved.
The people who actually do the work, as distinct from those who plan it.
The founders of a company, whether or not they still hold a formal role in it.
The layer of managers sitting between the front line and the people who set the strategy.
Everyone in a company who is not part of the leadership team, spoken of as a single body.
